transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-27
Start: 14:00 PT | Duration: ~66 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Miguel Santos (Redwood CSM), Alicia Park (CISO - Granite Financial), Mark Brenner (Head of Infra), Sofia Ruiz (Cloud Security Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be imperfect): Discussed Private VPC deployment options, SOC 2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO integration, audit log retention, customer-managed KMS and HSM options, network isolation patterns (peering, transit gateway, NAT, firewall rules), ingress/egress controls and allowed egress list, suggested next steps include sending security artifacts and diagram.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining - appreciate you making time. We'll do a security deep dive today, Priya will run us through the network and infra patterns, and then we'll leave time for questions.
[00:22] Alicia Park: Thanks Jordan, yeah Alicia here, I'm primarily focused on compliance and data residency. We're evaluating Redwood Private because we need strict controls and auditability.
[00:30] Jordan Lee: Great, can you remind us of the high level constraints? Data residency, SOC 2 scope, any on-prem requirements?
[00:42] Alicia Park: Sure. We need all customer PII to stay in our region - US-East and a subset in EU for our European customers. SOC 2 Type II is required, and we may require an on-prem option for the payment reconciliation service. We use Okta for SSO and SCIM for provisioning.
[01:05] Mark Brenner: Also important: our egress policy is very strict - outbound connections must go through approved egress firewall and we only allow connect to a small set of broker endpoints.
[01:18] Priya Nair: Understood. Quick note - our Private deployment supports VPC peering and transit gateway options, customer-managed VPCs, and an on-prem package. For KMS, you can use a customer-managed KMS key (cloud KMS) or an HSM for on-prem. We can show an example KMS workflow.
[01:38] Sofia Ruiz: When you say HSM for on-prem, do you support HSM over n- like do you have an appliance integration or is it a KMIP bridge?
[01:45] Priya Nair: We typically integrate via KMIP or a supported HSM API; for cloud we support customer-managed keys in AWS KMS/CloudHSM. For on-prem we can do a direct HSM or proxy that we deploy into your network. There's a slight variation depending on air-gap requirements.
[02:09] Jordan Lee: We'll attach the exact models and docs, but Priya can show network diagram now.
[02:20] Priya Nair: Cool. I'm going to share a sample VPC architecture - imagine two subnets: control plane subnet (private) and worker subnet. The control plane is in our private control plane -- sorry, let me rephrase - for Private deployment the control plane can be customer-managed or Redwood-hosted inside the customer's VPC via peering. We support both patterns.
[02:45] Priya Nair: Option A: VPC peering - Redwood runs inference nodes in a dedicated VPC and we peer to customer VPC. All traffic stays on AWS backbone. You manage security groups and NACLs on your side. Option B: Transit gateway - recommended for multi-account setups. Option C: On-prem package - runs in your datacenter behind your firewall with optional air-gap.
[03:10] Mark Brenner: For peering, how do you handle ingress? We need to ensure we control inbound to the worker subnet and no unexpected ports are opened.
[03:20] Priya Nair: Good question. We only require outbound connections from the worker nodes to Redwood control endpoints for updates and health checks - those can be restricted by destination IP and TLS. For inbound, we don't open arbitrary ports into your network - we rely on mutual TLS for control plane connections and we can use private endpoints so no public internet path is needed.
[03:44] Sofia Ruiz: You mentioned private endpoints - do you mean VPC endpoints or private link?
[03:49] Priya Nair: We support VPC endpoints (Interface endpoints/PrivateLink) and can expose the inference API via a private endpoint in your VPC. That avoids public ingress and enforces egress rules.
[04:05] Alicia Park: Auditability is huge for us - we need audit logs for every request, with request metadata, who invoked it, and retention for 7 years for certain classes. Does Redwood provide per-request audit logs and can we ship them to our SIEM?
[04:21] Miguel Santos: Yes - log streaming is supported. We can stream audit logs to customer S3 buckets or to your SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch/HTTP. Retention length is configurable on your side; we can also provide a longer-term archival option. The logs include request id, user id, model version, and tokens - note token content may be subject to PII masking if enabled.
[04:48] Mark Brenner: Is there a way to avoid storing full prompt text in logs?
[04:52] Priya Nair: Yes, you can enable prompt redaction or hashing. We offer configurable redaction at ingestion and you can route raw logs only to your S3 if you want to retain full content under your control.
[05:06] Jordan Lee: Quick note on SOC2 and ISO - we will share our SOC2 Type II report and ISO27001 compliance summary. Those are typical asks.
[05:16] Alicia Park: Good. Also SSO: we need SAML/Okta integration and SCIM for provisioning, plus RBAC. Can you map Redwood roles to our LDAP groups?
[05:28] Priya Nair: We support SAML SSO with Okta and SCIM provisioning. Role mapping can be done via SAML attributes or SCIM group sync. We also have RBAC with fine-grained roles for admin, operator, and auditor.
[05:45] Sofia Ruiz: I'd like to see an example for auditor role so they have read-only access to logs and metrics but cannot invoke models.
[05:52] Miguel Santos: We'll provide sample RBAC policies and an example JSON mapping.
[06:02] Mark Brenner: Let's dig deeper on network egress. Our security team wants to limit all worker egress to specific FQDNs and only via our egress firewall. Can Redwood operate in a model where we only allow outbound to a small approved set?
[06:18] Priya Nair: Yes - the worker nodes only need to reach specific endpoints for model artifacts, telemetry, and the control plane. We can provide a published list of FQDNs/IPs for allowed egress. In strict environments we recommend hosting artifacts in your account (S3) so you can avoid external egress.
[06:37] Alicia Park: For model artifacts: can we host model weights in our S3 so they never traverse the public internet?
[06:44] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Model weights can be stored in customer buckets and Redwood worker nodes will pull from there across the peering or via private endpoints.
[06:53] Sofia Ruiz: How do you do image signing or integrity checks for model weights?
[06:58] Priya Nair: We support signed manifests and checksum verification. We also track model versioning and provide a manifest with a cryptographic hash so you can verify integrity.
[07:12] Mark Brenner: What about network segmentation inside the VPC? We run multiple workloads and we want to isolate Redwood workers into dedicated subnets and security groups.
[07:20] Priya Nair: That's standard. We recommend dedicated subnets, security groups with deny-by-default, and a dedicated route table. We also support restricted IAM roles for node access and we can provide a bastion pattern for admin maintenance.
[07:36] Jordan Lee: Priya, can you walk through a sample firewall rule set for ingress/egress?
[07:40] Priya Nair: Sure - inbound: no open inbound on 0.0.0.0/0. For control plane we allow inbound from Redwood control plane CIDR via the peering connection and only specific ports (443 for HTTPS, 8443 for metrics if needed). Outbound: allow TCP 443 to specific FQDNs/IP ranges for artifact downloads, and allow to your SIEM endpoints for log streaming. We also recommend NACL deny rules for any ephemeral ranges.
[08:15] Sofia Ruiz: Do you offer mutual TLS between our services and the worker nodes?
[08:20] Priya Nair: Yes we support mTLS for service-to-service communication. We can provision certificates via your PKI or integrate with your ACME flow.
[08:33] Mark Brenner: For on-prem, what's the upgrade story? We want automated updates but under our control.
[08:40] Priya Nair: For on-prem we support a staged update process - we push images to your air-gapped registry or we provide signed packages. You get a canary deploy window and you control when to pull updates.
[08:55] Jordan Lee: A few times people asked about KV cache - that's internal caching of model context, right? Any special considerations?
[09:02] Priya Nair: Correct - KV cache stays on the worker node ephemeral storage. It's not persisted to long-term storage unless you opt into snapshotting. We encrypt ephemeral disks and rotate disk keys.
[09:14] Alicia Park: Disk encryption - do you support customer-managed disk keys?
[09:18] Priya Nair: Yes, you can supply keys or use customer-managed KMS for EBS encryption in AWS. For on-prem we can integrate with HSM.
[09:28] Miguel Santos: Also note we support per-tenant encryption context so logs and artifacts are encrypted with tenant-specific KEKs.
[09:36] Sofia Ruiz: What about secrets management for model prompts or API keys - can they live in our Vault?
[09:41] Priya Nair: Yes, Redwood supports integration with HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or your key store. We never persist raw secrets in plaintext; secret access is ephemeral and audited.
[09:55] Mark Brenner: Let's cover SSO flow - we use Okta and require SCIM provisioning. Can the Redwood console authenticate against our IdP for admin and operator roles?
[10:04] Priya Nair: Yes - SAML SSO integration for the console is standard. SCIM provisioning creates user accounts and groups. We can map Okta groups to Redwood roles.
[10:16] Alicia Park: Are service principals supported for machine-to-machine access with scoped permissions?
[10:20] Jordan Lee: Yes, we have API keys and short-lived tokens via workload identity - you can bind them to IAM roles and scoping. We also support OIDC-based workload identity for fine-grained machine auth.
[10:35] Sofia Ruiz: Can we audit token issuance?
[10:37] Miguel Santos: Yes all token issuance and revocation events are logged in audit trail.
[10:42] Priya Nair: Quick pause - any burning networking questions?
[10:47] Mark Brenner: One more: how do you prevent data exfiltration if a worker is compromised? E.g., rate-limited egress?
[10:57] Priya Nair: Primary controls: restrictive egress to approved endpoints only, VPC flow logs to detect anomalies, host-based controls and process isolation on worker containers, and we can integrate with your DLP. We also recommend turning on network flow monitoring and alerting.
[11:18] Sofia Ruiz: For VPC flow logs and packet captures, do you stream to our monitoring?
[11:22] Priya Nair: Yes, we can forward flow logs to your collector, or you can enable VPC flow logs in your account and we can analyze them as part of the observability bundle.
[11:32] Jordan Lee: On the compliance side - SOC 2: we provide Type II report and can do an in-person audit if needed for enterprise deals. ISO documentation is available too.
[11:41] Alicia Park: Good to know. For contract clauses, we need a data processing addendum and specific language for subprocessor list. Do you maintain a subprocessor registry?
[11:52] Miguel Santos: Yes, we maintain a subprocessors list and can provide a DPA with standard EU addendum and any required appendices.
[12:00] Priya Nair: Quick note on network isolation for on-prem - we can run a full appliance in your datacenter, with local control of ingress/egress, and no outbound internet if required. In that mode we rely on your patching and local operations, with Redwood providing signed binaries and runbooks.
[12:20] Mark Brenner: For the appliance, is there an embedded HSM or do we need to provide one?
[12:26] Priya Nair: We can support both. We can ship with an embedded HSM module or integrate with your existing HSM via KMIP. There is a secure enclave option too.
[12:37] Alicia Park: A few compliance-specific items: log immutability, tamper-evidence, and retention controls. How are logs guaranteed immutable?
[12:48] Miguel Santos: For immutability we recommend streaming logs into a write-once S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled and MFA delete if needed. We can also provide signed log digests that are append-only.
[13:05] Sofia Ruiz: On data residency - if we mirror EU customers to EU region, does Redwood maintain separate model instances?
[13:12] Priya Nair: Yes - we can pin model instances to regions, and your data never leaves the region if configured that way. We can do regional routing and fallbacks only to in-region models.
[13:26] Mark Brenner: Any third-party penetration testing history? We need results or an attestation.
[13:33] Jordan Lee: We run regular pen tests and can share the executive summary. For deeper access we can consider a joint test arrangement per contract.
[13:44] Alicia Park: Network hardening recommendations?
[13:47] Priya Nair: Harden nodes with CIS benchmarks, disable unused ports, enforce EDR on hosts, and run container scanning for images.
[13:55] Sofia Ruiz: Do you have example iptables/firewall rules to lock down egress?
[13:59] Priya Nair: Yes - the runbook includes sample security group rules, NACL examples, and a minimal allowed egress list.
[14:08] Mark Brenner: On TLS - we require TLS1.2 minimum and prefer 1.3. What does Redwood enforce?
[14:13] Priya Nair: We enforce TLS1.2+ and support TLS1.3; we can configure ciphers per customer in the private deployment.
[14:27] Jordan Lee: Time check - we have about 50 minutes left; want to deep dive on any of these topics?
[14:33] Alicia Park: Let's walk through a concrete data flow for a request - start at customer app -> through our LB -> egress to Redwood worker -> model inference -> response. We want to see where logs are emitted and what touches PII.
[14:49] Priya Nair: Sure. Step 1: Client -> internal LB (authenticated with mTLS or API key). Step 2: LB forwards to an endpoint in the customer VPC that routes to Redwood worker via VPC peering/private endpoint. Step 3: Worker pulls model weights from customer S3 if configured, or from Redwood artifact store via private link. Step 4: Inference occurs; ephemeral KV cache used for context. Step 5: Response returned to client via the same path; audit log event emitted and forwarded to your SIEM or S3. PII handling: we can mask or redact PII at ingestion and you control whether full prompts are kept.
[15:25] Sofia Ruiz: What about multi-tenant isolation between different customers on shared infra?
[15:29] Priya Nair: For hosted Shared infra we use strict tenant isolation with separate namespaces and encryption keys per tenant. For Private we typically run dedicated worker pools for a tenant, removing shared tenancy concerns.
[15:44] Mark Brenner: Understood. For the dedicated worker pool, what's the blast radius if a tenant is compromised?
[15:50] Priya Nair: Reduced - dedicated pools mean compromised tenant can't access other tenants' data. We also enforce process-level isolation and network segmentation.
[15:59] Jordan Lee: A few folks asked about metrics/observability - can we forward Prometheus metrics to your collector or do you provide push gateways?
[16:08] Priya Nair: We provide metrics endpoints and can push to your monitoring or you can pull via read-only endpoints. Logs and metrics can be configured to route to your cluster.
[16:18] Miguel Santos: Also, tracing for request correlation is supported - we include request id in logs for end-to-end chain.
[16:26] Alicia Park: Let's capture known risks: data in transit, disk at rest, key management, and supply-chain risk of model weights.
[16:35] Priya Nair: Agreed. Mitigations: TLS/mTLS, customer-managed KMS, audit logs, signed manifests, and SBOMs for runtime images.
[16:44] Sofia Ruiz: One more on host isolation - do you run worker containers as unprivileged users?
[16:49] Priya Nair: Yes, containers run with least privilege; we don't run as root by default. We also enforce seccomp and AppArmor profiles on supported platforms.
[17:00] Mark Brenner: For firewalling, what does the default look like?
[17:04] Priya Nair: Deny all inbound; outbound only to allowed FQDNs/IPs on 443; control-plane initiated connections are over private peering; NACLs with explicit deny; Security groups with minimal open ports.
[17:18] Jordan Lee: Quick clarifying Q from sales - is there any scenario where customer data leaves the region without explicit config?
[17:25] Priya Nair: No - by default data stays in the region. Cross-region replication only occurs with explicit customer opt-in.
[17:34] Alicia Park: Can you provide me with the list of subprocessors for our DPA review?
[17:38] Miguel Santos: Yes - we'll attach the subprocessors registry in the follow-up email.
[17:45] Priya Nair: I'll share the runbook with sample iptables and security group templates.
[17:50] Sofia Ruiz: For the private peering, do you use AWS PrivateLink for API traffic or VPC Peering?
[17:56] Priya Nair: We support both. PrivateLink is recommended when you want interface endpoints and tighter control; peering is simple for VPC-to-VPC. For multi-account architectures transit gateway is often best.
[18:10] Mark Brenner: Anything about IP whitelisting?
[18:13] Priya Nair: Yes we offer IP whitelisting per customer and can provide a static egress IP range for allowed firewall rules.
[18:24] Jordan Lee: Time check again - do we need to demo anything live or are we ok with artifacts?
[18:30] Alicia Park: Artifacts and the SOC reports first. Then we'll schedule a POC for the on-prem appliance if the DPA looks good.
[18:38] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Any remaining questions?
[18:41] Sofia Ruiz: A few small clarifications about key rotation - how often does Redwood rotate keys and can we enforce rotation windows?
[18:49] Priya Nair: We rotate platform keys quarterly and support customer-initiated rotation. For customer-managed KMS you control rotation windows.
[18:58] Mark Brenner: For the HSM integration, do you support split-key or dual-control for key access?
[19:03] Priya Nair: Yes we can integrate with HSMs that support split-key and dual-control workflows.
[19:12] Alicia Park: Last one: do you have an incident response playbook we can review?
[19:17] Miguel Santos: Yes - we'll attach the IR runbook including contact paths, SLA for incident response, and forensic capabilities.
[19:27] Jordan Lee: Ok, let's recap and close. Next steps: we'll send SOC2, ISO docs, subprocessors, networking runbook, and sample VPC diagrams. Priya will send firewall examples. We'll schedule a follow-up week of 11/3 for infra deep dive.
[19:45] Alicia Park: Great, thanks everyone.
[19:47] Mark Brenner: Thanks all.
[19:49] Sofia Ruiz: Thanks.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mislabels and ASR errors possible (e.g., K V cache vs KV cache, V P C vs VPC).
